newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Sick Yeltsin wants branches of power to cooperate.
newsitem.headline: Sick Yeltsin wants branches of power to cooperate.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, anxious to avert political confrontation before he goes under the surgeon's knife, on Monday called for closer cooperation between Russia's government, the Kremlin and parliament.
Yeltsin, 65, readying himself for heart bypass surgery next month, proposed that the top four officials from the branches of power get together regularly to prepare decisions.

The Kremlin chief's proposal appeared intended to limit confrontation as he awaits his operation and to repair divisions opened by security chief Alexander Lebed before his sacking last week after four months in the Kremlin.
Yeltsin told Gennady Seleznyov, the communist speaker of the State Duma lower house of parliament, that the various branches of power needed to pull together to face tough challenges.

"These are our common tasks, our common problems, and at this moment in time we cannot have people running in different directions and solving questions in their own ways," Yeltsin said during a 30-minute meeting with Seleznyov.
Televised excerpts from the meeting at the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow, made available by the presidential press service, showed Yeltsin speaking confidently, loudly and relatively clearly.
He is due to be operated on in mid-November.
Yeltsin's spokesman, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, told a Kremlin briefing that Yeltsin and Seleznyov had agreed that a new "permanent four" would meet regularly.
They would be Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais, Seleznyov and Yegor Stroyev, the speaker of the Federation Council upper chamber.
"In the current situation such meetings could become an effective mechanism to search for agreed solutions to the most important issues of the country's life," Yastrzhembsky said.

The State Duma is largely hostile to Yeltsin. The Federation Council has many Yeltsin appointees but the latest in a series of regional elections on Sunday returned some candidates opposed to the president, including former arch foe Alexander Rutskoi.

Rutskoi, who led a hardline parliamentary rebellion against Yeltsin in 1993 and was briefly jailed, was elected governor of the central Kursk region by a landslide to complete a remarkable political comeback.
Seleznyov told reporters that Yeltsin would take over from Chubais on the "permanent four" after he had recovered from his heart operation, but Yastrzhembsky made no mention of this.
Yastrzhembsky's omission could prompt speculation that Chubais is increasing his influence in Yeltsin's absence.
Although Yeltsin has now rid himself of Lebed -- who openly aspired to become president -- the other main players in the succession stakes are still jockeying for position.

But Seleznyov said Yeltsin still had a firm grip on the levers of power. "Despite his illness, he is in control of the situation and is taking decisions by himself. I think he has information on eveything going on in the country," he told reporters.
The Kremlin leader, deeply unhappy about Lebed's behaviour, sacked the outspoken general last week and replaced him with moderate former Duma speaker Ivan Rybkin.

Chernomyrdin introduced Rybkin on Monday to his colleagues on the Security Council -- which groups top defence, security and state leaders and is headed by Yeltsin -- and told him to find a way to permanently settle the 21-month Chechnya conflict.
Chernomyrdin said he wanted a peaceful solution to the conflict, in which tens of thousands of people have died, but ruled out any prospect of Chechnya being allowed to secede.
